name: Special senses
description: The eye and vision, the ear, hearing and balance, and smell, taste and touch: structures, how each sense works, the nerves that carry it and common disorders. Pictures show the eyeballs, optic nerves, outer ear and nasal cartilages to name; BodyParts3D has no lens, retina, inner ear, ossicles or tongue models, so those are text questions.

source.name: Written for Study Buddy. Pictures rendered from BodyParts3D (© The Database Center for Life Science, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP).

questions.prompt: Which organs are highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: Each eye sits in a bony socket, the orbit, cushioned by fat.

figure.alt: The two eyeballs, in red, in their sockets in the skull seen from the front
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: What is the bony socket that holds the eyeball called?
questions.explanation: Made of seven bones: frontal, zygomatic, maxilla, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal and palatine.

figure.alt: The two eyeballs, in red, in their sockets
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: What are the three layers (tunics) of the wall of the eyeball, from outside in?
answers: Fibrous (sclera and cornea), vascular (choroid, ciliary body, iris), neural (retina)
questions.explanation: Fibrous tunic, vascular tunic (uvea), nervous tunic.

questions.prompt: What is the tough white outer coat of the eyeball called?
questions.explanation: It gives the eye its shape, and the eye muscles attach to it.

questions.prompt: What is the clear window at the front of the eye, which does most of the focusing, called?
questions.explanation: It supplies about two thirds of the eye's focusing power. It has no blood vessels.

questions.prompt: What is the thin clear membrane over the front of the eye and inside the eyelids called?
questions.explanation: 'Pink eye' is an inflammation of it.

questions.prompt: Which dark, blood-rich layer between the sclera and the retina feeds the retina and absorbs stray light?
What is the coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil called?
questions.explanation: The pupil is the hole in its centre.

questions.prompt: What happens to the pupil in bright light?
questions.explanation: The sphincter pupillae muscle contracts, supplied by the parasympathetic oculomotor nerve. In the dark, the sympathetic dilator pupillae widens it.

questions.prompt: Which clear, flexible structure behind the iris changes shape to focus on near and far objects?
questions.explanation: There is no model of it in the picture set.

questions.prompt: To look at something close, what do the lens and ciliary muscle do?
answers: The ciliary muscle contracts and the lens gets rounder
The lens becomes thicker and rounder
wrong: The ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens flattens
questions.explanation: For distance the ciliary muscle relaxes, the suspensory ligaments pull tight and the lens is flat.

questions.prompt: What is the watery fluid in the front of the eye, made by the ciliary body, called?
questions.explanation: It drains through the canal of Schlemm. Blocked drainage raises the pressure, which is glaucoma.

questions.prompt: What is the clear jelly that fills the large space behind the lens called?
questions.explanation: It keeps the retina against the back of the eye.

questions.prompt: Which layer at the back of the eye holds the light-sensitive cells?
What is the difference between rods and cones?
answers: Rods work in dim light; cones give colour vision and detail in bright light
Rods see in the dark; cones see colour
wrong: Rods see colour; cones see in the dark
Rods are in the lens; cones are in the retina
Rods detect sound; cones detect light
questions.explanation: About 120 million rods and 6 million cones in each eye.

questions.prompt: Which small pit in the macula, packed with cones, gives the sharpest vision?
questions.explanation: We turn the eye so that what we look at falls on it.

questions.prompt: Why is there a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the eye?
answers: There are no rods or cones there
No photoreceptors at the optic disc
questions.explanation: The brain fills the gap, so we do not notice.

questions.prompt: Which cells are affected in colour blindness?
questions.explanation: Mostly in the red or green cones. More common in men, as the genes are on the X chromosome.

questions.prompt: Lack of which vitamin causes night blindness?
questions.explanation: Needed to make rhodopsin, the pigment in the rods.

questions.prompt: Which structures are highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: They carry the signals of the retina to the brain, crossing at the optic chiasm.

figure.alt: The optic nerves and tracts seen from below, in red, under the brain
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: What is the order of the visual pathway, from the eye to the cortex?
answers: Optic nerve, chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, visual cortex
Optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, thalamus, occipital lobe
wrong: Optic nerve, thalamus, chiasm, tract, cortex
Optic tract, chiasm, nerve, cortex, thalamus
Optic nerve, chiasm, tract, cerebellum, cortex
questions.explanation: The visual cortex is in the occipital lobe.

questions.prompt: At the optic chiasm, which fibres cross to the other side?
answers: Those from the nasal half of each retina
wrong: Those from the temporal half of each retina
questions.explanation: So each side of the brain sees the opposite half of the visual field.

questions.prompt: How many extraocular muscles move each eye?
questions.explanation: Four rectus (superior, inferior, medial, lateral) and two oblique (superior, inferior).

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerves supply the eye muscles?
questions.explanation: 'LR6 SO4': the lateral rectus is supplied by VI, the superior oblique by IV, all the others by III.

questions.prompt: Which gland above the outer corner of the eye makes tears?
questions.explanation: Tears drain through the puncta into the nasolacrimal duct, to the nose.

questions.prompt: What are the jobs of tears?
answers: They wash and moisten the eye, and kill germs with lysozyme
Moisten, clean and protect the cornea
wrong: They carry blood to the cornea
questions.explanation: The runny nose when we cry comes from the nasolacrimal duct.

questions.prompt: In short sight (myopia), where does the light from a distant object focus?
questions.explanation: The eyeball is too long. A concave lens corrects it.

questions.prompt: In long sight (hyperopia), where does the light from a near object focus?
questions.explanation: The eyeball is too short. A convex lens corrects it.

questions.prompt: What is a clouding of the lens, common in older people, called?
questions.explanation: Treated by replacing the lens with an artificial one.

questions.prompt: Which eye disease, caused by raised pressure that damages the optic nerve, first narrows the field of vision?
Which part of the ear is highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: The ear flap of elastic cartilage and skin. It collects the sound and directs it into the ear canal.

figure.alt: The outer ear, in red, on the side of the head
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: What are the three parts of the ear?
questions.explanation: Only the inner ear, in the temporal bone, holds the receptors.

questions.prompt: What is the tube from the auricle to the eardrum, about 2.5 cm long, called?
questions.explanation: It has hairs and wax glands.

questions.prompt: What does the tympanic membrane (eardrum) do?
answers: It vibrates with the sound and passes it to the ossicles
wrong: It turns sound into nerve signals
questions.explanation: It separates the outer and middle ear.

questions.prompt: What are the three tiny bones of the middle ear called, in order from the eardrum?
questions.explanation: The smallest bones in the body. They pass the vibrations on and make them stronger.

questions.prompt: Which is the smallest bone in the body, in the middle ear?
questions.explanation: Its footplate fits into the oval window of the cochlea.

questions.prompt: Which tube connects the middle ear to the throat and evens out the air pressure?
questions.explanation: It opens when we swallow or yawn.

questions.prompt: Why do small children get middle ear infections so often?
answers: Their auditory tubes are short and horizontal, so germs pass from the throat
The tube from the throat is short and flat

questions.prompt: Which snail-shaped organ of the inner ear contains the receptors for hearing?
questions.explanation: It has about 2.75 turns.

questions.prompt: What is the organ with the sound-sensitive hair cells inside the cochlea called?
How is sound turned into nerve signals in the cochlea?
answers: Fluid waves bend the hair cells, which fire the cochlear nerve
Hair cells are bent by waves in the fluid
wrong: The eardrum fires the nerve directly
The semicircular canals sense the pitch
questions.explanation: Different parts of the cochlea respond to different pitches: the base to high, the apex to low.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries signals of hearing and balance?
Which structures in the inner ear sense rotation of the head?
questions.explanation: There are three, in the three planes. The cristae in their ampullae detect it.

questions.prompt: Which organs of the inner ear, the utricle and saccule, sense the head's position and straight-line movement?
questions.explanation: Tiny crystals of calcium carbonate, otoliths, lie on the hair cells.

questions.prompt: Which word means a false sense that the world is spinning, often from a fault in the inner ear?
What is a ringing in the ears, with no outside sound, called?
What is the difference between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss?
answers: Conductive is a problem in the outer or middle ear; sensorineural is in the cochlea or nerve
Conductive involves the ossicles or eardrum; sensorineural, the inner ear or nerve
wrong: Conductive is a fault of the brain; sensorineural, of the ear canal
Conductive means loss from age; sensorineural, from noise
questions.explanation: Wax in the ear canal is a common cause of conductive loss.

questions.prompt: What is age-related hearing loss, starting with the high pitches, called?
At about what level of sound does prolonged exposure start to damage the hair cells?
questions.explanation: A busy street is about 80 dB; a rock concert about 110 dB.

questions.prompt: Which structures are highlighted in red?
questions.explanation: They shape the lower part of the nose. Only the bridge is bone.

figure.alt: The cartilages of the nose, in red, seen from the front over the skull
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Which part of the nose is bony, and which cartilaginous?
answers: The bridge is bone (nasal bones); the tip and the sides below are cartilage
Upper part bone, lower part cartilage
wrong: The tip is bone, the bridge is cartilage
All of the nose is bone
All of the nose is cartilage
questions.explanation: A blow to the nose often breaks the nasal bones.

figure.alt: The cartilages of the nose, in red, seen from the side
figure.credit: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science

questions.prompt: Where are the receptors for smell found?
answers: In the olfactory epithelium at the roof of the nasal cavity
questions.explanation: About 10 million receptor cells. Their axons pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries the sense of smell?
questions.explanation: The olfactory bulbs lie under the frontal lobes. It is the only sense that reaches the cortex without passing through the thalamus first.

questions.prompt: Why can smells bring back strong memories and emotions?
answers: The olfactory pathway links directly to the limbic system
Smell goes straight to the limbic system
wrong: The nose is next to the hippocampus
Smell is carried by the vagus nerve
The cochlea is next to the olfactory bulb

questions.prompt: What do the nasal conchae (turbinates) do?
answers: They warm, moisten and clean the air as it passes
questions.explanation: Three on each side: superior, middle and inferior.

questions.prompt: What are the air-filled spaces in the skull bones around the nose called?
questions.explanation: Frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary. They lighten the skull and add resonance to the voice.

questions.prompt: Where are the taste buds mostly found?
answers: On the papillae of the tongue
questions.explanation: About 10 000, with some on the palate and throat.

questions.prompt: Which kind of papillae on the tongue have no taste buds, and give the surface its rough feel?
questions.explanation: They are the most numerous.

questions.prompt: Which five basic tastes can we detect?
answers: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami
wrong: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and spicy
Sweet, sour, salty and bitter only
Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and cold
questions.explanation: 'Spicy' is a pain sensation. Umami is the savoury taste of glutamate.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerves carry the sense of taste?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve serves the front two thirds of the tongue and the glossopharyngeal the back third.

questions.prompt: Why does food seem tasteless when you have a cold?
answers: Much of flavour comes from smell
questions.explanation: The smell of the food reaches the olfactory epithelium from the back of the mouth.

questions.prompt: Which receptors in the skin detect light touch?
questions.explanation: Dense in the fingertips and lips.

questions.prompt: What kind of receptor senses pain?
questions.explanation: Mostly free nerve endings.

questions.prompt: What is the sense of the position of the body and limbs called?
questions.explanation: From muscle spindles, tendon organs and joint receptors.

questions.prompt: What is sensory adaptation?
answers: The decline in the response of a receptor to a steady stimulus
Getting used to a constant stimulus
wrong: An increase in sensitivity to a steady stimulus
questions.explanation: Why we stop noticing a smell or the feel of our clothes.

questions.prompt: What is pain felt in a place away from its source, such as the left arm in a heart attack, called?
questions.explanation: The nerves from both areas join the same spinal cord segments.

tests.name: Name the part
tests.why: Pictures of the eyes, optic nerves, outer ear and nasal cartilages, each with one part in red to name.

tests.name: Chapter quiz
tests.why: Thirty questions from the whole chapter, marked at the end, like an end-of-unit test.

tests.name: Recall without choices
tests.why: Type each answer from memory, starting with the ones due for review. Small typos are forgiven.
